newsitem.title: USA: Economist Kaufman says interest rates should rise.
newsitem.headline: Economist Kaufman says interest rates should rise.

text.p: The Federal Reserve should raise interest rates soon, but probably will not do so in March, according to economist Henry Kaufman.
Kaufman, president of Henry Kaufman & Co Inc, an international investment management and economic consulting firm, said the Fed could wait until the end of April to raise rates.
The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), the policy making arm of the Fed, meets on March 25 and does not formally convene again until May 20.
But the Fed's asymmetrical policy directive, one that specifies a bias toward higher rates, would allow policy makers to adjust rates between meetings, Kaufman said.
Kaufman, former vice chairman of Salomon Inc and managing director of Salomon Brothers' research departments, correctly forecast the sharp interest-rate rise that occurred in the 1970s.
On August 17, 1982, Kaufman accurately predicted that interest rates would fall dramatically, a forecast that that day sent stock prices up by what was then a record amount.
The Fed rate hike that Kaufman now expects would be a marginal one of 25 basis points, but it would mark a monetary policy turn and would be followed by one or two other rate increases this year.
That means the Fed funds rate would be 5.75 percent or six percent and the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond yield will be between seven percent to 7-1/2 percent by yearend, he said.
Kaufman said the Fed should raise rates because economic activity is going to remain quite strong in 1997.
"The economy should achieve three precent real growth in the first quarter without too much difficulty," he said.
And looking past the first quarter, there is nothing standing in the way of economic growth as the year progresses.
Liquidity is plentiful, said Kaufman. "There are willing lenders and willing investors. Job growth continues so we will continue to have good consumption spending."
Kaufman said "reasonably good profit generation suggests that capital spending will again be quite good" this year.
"We are moving closer to the point at which there is some friction that will induce higher inflation numbers," he said.

"Those inflation numbers will not be dramatically higher, but somewhat higher, and it's the Fed's responsibility to look somewhat ahead, rather than to just base policy on current and immediately past economic conditions," Kaufman said.

The difficulty for the Fed is that while it is concerned about the inflationary pressures that a tight labor market could bring about, it "doesn't have strong evidence that the inflationary situation is heating up," Kaufman said.
So that it "does not get blamed for inducing a stock market selloff," the Fed will wait to raise rates until it has "a better batch of (economic data) to support what they do," Kaufman said.

The intent of the monetary policy change would be "to temper economic behavior and to hold in check economic excesses -- in particular to prevent a significant rise in the rate of inflation," Kaufman said.

Asked whether Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan had appropriately used the term "irrational exuberance" in the context of the stock market's performance, Kaufman said, "The equity market does display quite a bit of exuberance. Whether this exuberance is irrational or rational is highly debatable. But it would seem to me that if we do not yet have irrational exuberance, we're getting very close to it."
